title: Venus Has Giant Mystery Rings—And Scientists Just Got a 3D Peek!
summary: Have you ever seen a lava lamp? Blobs of hot wax rise up, cool, and sink. Venus, our neighbor planet, might have something similar happening under its surface! Scientists found 741 giant rings on Venus called coronae (say: kuh-ROH-nee). They can be as wide as the whole United States! Using old data from a NASA spacecraft, researchers made new 3D maps of these rings. They think the rings are made when super-hot material, like a magma plume, pushes up from deep inside Venus and stretches the crust. It's like a cosmic pimple! The maps show that 52 of these coronae might have warm goo rising underneath them right now. That means Venus could be more geologically active than we thought—maybe even with moving bits of crust, like Earth's plate tectonics. But Venus is super dry, so its rocks are stiff and don't slide around easily. On Earth, oceans helped make our rocks squishy enough to break into plates, which recycle carbon and keep our climate stable. Venus never had big oceans, so it's stuck. Future missions will get even better looks at these mysterious rings. Who knows what secrets they'll reveal about our twin planet?
why_it_matters: Finding that Venus might still be moving inside changes how we think about planets and helps us understand why Earth stayed friendly for life while Venus became a deadly oven.

background_read: Venus is almost the same size as Earth, so it's sometimes called our planet's twin—but it's extremely hot and has no oceans. A NASA spacecraft (the U.S. space agency) gathered the pictures that scientists recently turned into 3D maps. Earth's plate tectonics recycle carbon dioxide and keep our climate stable, but Venus's dry, stiff crust does not allow that, which might explain why it became so harsh.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists studying Venus and its mysterious rings
WHAT: They discovered 741 coronae and 3D maps showed some might be active with rising magma plumes
WHERE: On the surface of Venus, Earth's neighboring planet
WHY: To understand whether Venus is still geologically active and why it turned out so different from Earth

perspectives.description: They hope that an active Venus could teach us how planets evolve and why some, like Earth, stay livable while others do not.
They point out that the maps rely on old data, so a new spacecraft is needed to measure the heat and activity directly.
They are amazed that our 'sister planet' still has surprises, proving that even familiar neighbors can be mysterious.
